title: Rama breaks
hook: the hero weeps in the forest

segments.voice: Yesterday: the abduction, and Jatayu, the old bird who fought a king and lost his wings. Your line was he tried. Did you think of someone who tried for you? Day fifty-three.

Think of the strongest person you know. The one who holds the family together, who drives everyone to the hospital, who never seems to fall apart. Now picture the first time you saw them cry. Maybe at a funeral. Maybe in the car, when they thought nobody was looking. It changes something, doesn't it? It's frightening and it's a relief at the same time. The Ramayana has that moment. Rama, the prince who accepted exile in one sentence, who faced fourteen thousand warriors alone, walks back to the hut after chasing the golden deer. The door is open. The line in the dust is still there. And Sita is gone.
screen: `THE STRONGEST PERSON YOU KNOW.` → `THE FIRST TIME THEY CRIED.` → `THE HUT IS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: What happens next is one of the rawest passages in the whole poem, and it doesn't flatter its hero. Rama runs from tree to tree, calling her name, asking the trees whether they've seen her. He asks the river. He asks the deer, and in Valmiki's telling the deer all turn their heads and look south. He sees a flower and thinks it's her. He weeps until he can barely stand. Then the grief turns into rage. He tells Lakshmana he'll fill the sky with arrows and tear the worlds apart until the gods give her back. It's his younger brother, the one who's usually the hothead, who calms him down: you're the one who taught everyone patience, he says, in effect. Don't become the storm. Then they find Jatayu, and Rama holds the dying bird. So why would a story about a divine hero show him coming apart like this? Here's one answer the tradition gives, and it goes right back to how the poem began. Valmiki, the poet, was walking by a river and saw a hunter shoot one of a pair of cranes. The other bird cried over its mate, and Valmiki was so struck with grief, shoka in Sanskrit, that words came out of him in a new rhythm. That rhythm became the shloka, the verse the whole Ramayana is written in. The poem is literally born from grief. So of course its hero weeps. Many Hindus see Rama as God come to earth as a man, and this is part of what that means to them: he doesn't pretend to be above loss. The strongest one in the story breaks, and nobody thinks less of him for it.
screen: `RAMA ASKS THE TREES.` · `THE GRIEF TURNS TO RAGE.` · `LAKSHMANA CALMS THE STORM.` · `SHOKA BECAME SHLOKA: BORN FROM GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop. Think of a strong person in your life who is grieving something right now, or who grieved in front of you once. Don't try to fix it. Don't try to cheer them up. Just sit next to them in your mind, the way Lakshmana sits next to Rama. Let their sadness be there without rushing it along. If something of your own grief comes up, let it sit there too. Nobody has to be the strong one for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Rama breaks. The hero, in the empty forest, asking the trees where she went. The poem doesn't hide it.
Your line: even he wept. Today, if someone strong near you looks tired, don't ask them to be strong. Ask how they are, and wait for the real answer. Day fifty-three.

howItsDone: Rama's lament in the forest is recited and sung in Ramayana readings, and Ramlila performances often stage it as one of the most emotional scenes; many devotees speak of Rama's grief as part of his fully human life on earth.

fork.reveal: Lakshmana, usually the hothead, becomes the calm one: he reminds Rama of his own patience and turns him back toward the search.

original.note: Sanskrit: grief, sorrow. Tradition says Valmiki's shoka turned into the first shloka.

trapdoor: what you thought: heroes don't cry.
what it means: Rama, whom many Hindus see as God on earth, weeps and rages in the forest, and the poem honors it.
what a scholar hears: shoka, grief, became shloka, verse. the Ramayana's own opening tells of a poem born from a poet's sorrow over a bird.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Rama's search and lament; Lakshmana calms him, roughly sargas 60–66)

notes: The deer looking south, Rama mistaking flowers for Sita, and his threat to destroy the worlds are from the Aranya Kanda lament as remembered; sarga numbers vary by edition. Please confirm.
Lakshmana's counsel is paraphrased loosely ('in effect'); confirm it fairly reflects the text.
The shoka/shloka story is from Bala Kanda 2 (the krauncha birds). The script calls them cranes; some translate 'curlews'. Confirm.
'Many Hindus see Rama as God come to earth as a man' is stated as belief, not ranked; confirm wording suits the path.
